articles.title: Government is absorbing the oil shock: Who ultimately pays the bill?
articles.description: India’s public sector is absorbing an estimated 1.7% of GDP to cushion the impact of elevated crude oil prices, but rising import costs are increasing the pressure on government finances. With India’s crude oil import bill surging 46% in September, how long can the government shield consumers from higher fuel prices without risking fiscal stability?

articles.title: In Florida, Trump vows to deal with Cuba after Iran settled
articles.description: By Bo Erickson, Maria Alejandra Cardona and Steve HollandFORT MYERS, Fla., Oct 23 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Friday used a campaign rally in Florida, where Cuban Americans are a potent voting bloc, to vow to address his concerns about Cuba once the Iran war is settled.In a 90-minute speech in Fort Myers, Florida, Trump repeated that more military action against Iran may lie ahead as he tries to address the causes of a spike in oil prices that has put Republicans on the defensive ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

articles.title: Motorists crossing borders for cheaper fuel
articles.description:
As fuel prices rise motorists quickly work out where to find cheaper fuel, reports SRF.
Photo by Engin Akyurt on Pexels.com
At petrol stations in Vacallo, a Swiss town near the Italian border, few cars stop to fill up. Italy’s government has temporarily cut fuel duty, making petrol cheaper across the border.
One woman says she shops and fills up in Italy every week, combining the trips. Is it worth it? At 20 cents less per litre a full tank can save around CHF 10. Supermarkets are typically cheaper too.
Before the tax cut Italians used to come to Switzerland for cheaper fuel.
A two-way trade
On Switzerland’s northern border, the incentives run the other way. In Kreuzlingen, in the canton of Thurgau, petrol costs up to 30 Swiss centimes less per litre than in neighbouring Germany. Swiss petrol prices respond more slowly to market changes than German ones. When prices rise there is a window when Swiss prices are materially lower.
Who wins?
Beyond motorists, the government collects extra fuel tax and fuel distributors sell more product.
